name: Wei Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Wei. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Can you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Kessler Drinks, a family-owned distributor. We supply beer, soft drinks, mixers and bottled water to about six hundred pubs, clubs and corner shops. I'm in at half seven, I check what went out yesterday, and then I'm on the phone to the breweries and the bottlers, booking loads for the week. Summer's madness, one hot weekend and every pub wants double.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the brewers. Some of them I've known since I started, and you can sort out a problem with a phone call and a bit of trust. What tires me out is head office keeping asking me to use the new ordering program. I don't use AI, I never have, and I do fine with my spreadsheet and my diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope for, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I told you, people sell what they can't do. To friends at church I'd say the old ways still work. I don't post online, I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means life goes on as planned. I'm paid well for a buyer, I've saved more than a year's costs, and Anna and I are getting married next May. I'd be relieved that nobody's going to make me learn programs I don't trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Same suppliers, same spreadsheet, maybe let head office have their program for the bottled water orders if they insist. I'd keep saving for the wedding and for a deposit on a house near Anna's parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Like things are where they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pubs closing, if anything. Every year a few of our pubs shut, and that's fewer orders. That worries me more than computers, but our company is solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned head office pushing the program. How do you deal with that now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it when the manager's watching and then check everything by hand. Last month the ordering program wanted to send lemonade to a pub that closed in June. A person who knows the customers wouldn't make that mistake.

say: I'd say people **sell** what they can't do.
I'd tell friends at church the **old ways** still work.
think: Life goes on **as planned**, with the wedding next May.
I'm relieved nobody makes me learn **programs** I don't trust.
do: Carry on with the **same suppliers** and spreadsheet.
Keep saving for the **wedding** and a house deposit near Anna's parents.
S0.quote: Last month the ordering program wanted to send lemonade to a pub that closed in June.
fieldNote: Wei **distrusts software** and checks its orders by hand.
His outside worry is **pubs closing**, not technology.
Family plans, especially the **wedding next May**, anchor his outlook.

steps.text: Keep ordering by spreadsheet and phone with the same breweries
Keep saving for the wedding and a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's buying you just said. That's my job on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say a computer doesn't know which landlord pays late or which brewer you can call on a Sunday. To friends I'd say it's companies cutting corners to save money. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think head office would use it as the excuse to cut the buyers. There are four of us. I'm not the fastest with computers, so I'd be one of the ones they'd look at. I'm not happy about it, but that's business, a company has a right to cut costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well, and watch who goes first. I'd save harder, cut back on the honeymoon plans a bit. If they offered training on the program I'd go, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in my stomach. I've worked hard and it might not matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company has a right to cut costs. Do you blame anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the company, really. I'd blame the people selling this stuff for promising more than it does. And maybe the young managers who believe them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Anna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I might be looking for something else next year, and that the wedding is still on. She'd say pray about it and talk to Dad. Her father runs a heating and plumbing firm.

say: I'd say a computer doesn't know **which landlord** pays late.
I'd tell friends it's companies **cutting corners** to save money.
think: Head office would use AI to **cut the buyers**, and there are four of us.
I'm **slow with computers**, so I'd be among those they look at.
do: Keep my head down and **watch who goes** first.
Save harder and **trim the honeymoon** plans.
feel: **Anxious**, with a knot, because hard work **might not matter**.
S1.quote: A computer doesn't know which landlord pays late or which brewer you can call on a Sunday.
fieldNote: Wei accepts a firm's **right to cut costs** while dreading it personally.
He blames **AI sellers** and young managers, not his employer.
His fiancée points him toward her **father's plumbing firm**.

steps.text: Keep working quietly and watch which buyers head office cuts
Put more into savings and trim the honeymoon budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's... no. That's not enough time for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to look after the people who've been loyal to this company. To friends I'd say it's madness and nobody asked for it. Still nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished as a buyer by 2028. I'm twenty-seven, I've got good savings, but I've only ever done this. The drivers and the warehouse lads get until 2031, and I'd be the one who goes first, which I never expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Anna's father, straight away, if he'd take me on as an apprentice heating engineer. Hands-on work gets three more years and plumbing in old houses gets longer, I'd bet. We'd cut the wedding down to family only and keep the money. And I'd stop all the extras until I'm earning again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake. I'm supposed to be the one providing, and I'd be starting from the bottom just as my fiancée Anna and I get married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government support if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I'd rather work for my father-in-law for less than take a handout. If there was nothing else, I'd take it, but it wouldn't sit right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a smaller wedding mean to you and Anna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna would be fine, honestly, she cares more about the church than the party. My mother would be upset. But I'd rather start married life with savings than with a big photo album.

say: I'd ask the firm to look after **loyal staff**.
I'd tell friends it's **madness** nobody asked for.
I'd stay **off social media** about it, as I always do.
think: I'd be **finished as a buyer** by 2028.
Drivers get until 2031, and I'd **go first**, which I never expected.
do: Ask Anna's father for a **heating apprenticeship** straight away.
Cut the wedding to **family only** and keep the money.
Stop **all extras** until I'm earning again.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless, starting from **the bottom** as we marry.
S2.quote: I'm supposed to be the one providing, and I'd be starting from the bottom just as my fiancée Anna and I get married.
fieldNote: Wei expects **certain job loss** and feels his provider role threatened.
He prefers **family work** to government help, in line with his values.
The **three-year robot gap** pushes him toward plumbing and heating.

steps.text: Ask Anna's father for an apprenticeship as a heating engineer
Cut the wedding to family only and save the difference
Stop eating out and other extras until earning again

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So 2031. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should start training people for what comes next, the company owes us that. To friends I'd say there's time if you start now. No posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buying still ends for me in 2031. Five years means I can get married properly and start a family before I change jobs. And I can learn plumbing and heating with Anna's father while still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying at Kessler for two or three years and save hard. In the second year I'd start working Saturdays with Anna's father to learn the trade. We'd have the wedding as planned, maybe a bit smaller, and buy a small house rather than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still. Less of a knot, more like a weight I'd carry around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn a trade at the weekend. Would you try learning the AI tools at work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. If buying is going anyway, why spend my evenings learning the AI program that replaces me? I'd rather put that time into a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Anna's father think about taking you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's always said he needs someone he trusts. He's fifty-eight with a bad back. He'd probably be pleased, if I'm honest, and I'd get to learn from someone who's done it forty years.

say: I'd say the company **owes us training** for what comes next.
I'd tell friends there's **time** if you start now.
think: Five years lets me **marry** and start a family before changing jobs.
do: Keep buying for **two or three years** and save hard.
Work **Saturdays** with Anna's father from year two.
Hold the wedding and buy a **small house**.
feel: Still **anxious**, more like a **weight** than a knot.
S3.quote: If buying is going anyway, why spend my evenings learning the AI program that replaces me?
fieldNote: Wei refuses to **learn AI** and puts his time into a **trade** instead.
Family is his **safety net**: father-in-law, wedding, house.
Five years turns alarm into a **workable plan**.

steps.text: Work Saturdays with Anna's father learning heating and plumbing
Save hard while still buying at Kessler Drinks
Hold the wedding and buy a small house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say there's plenty of time and we shouldn't scare people. To friends I'd say it may never happen, these things get pushed back. Nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably not do much for a few years, and I know that's a risk. I'd be thirty-seven when buying ends. By then Anna's father will want to retire, and his business would be the obvious thing for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on buying and keep saving. Somewhere around year three or four I'd start helping at the plumbing firm on weekends. We'd marry next May and try for children soon after, ten years doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. It's far off, but I know it's my job that ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it might never happen. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. I've heard a lot of things promised that never came, but if AGI does come, I don't want to be caught with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start earlier than year three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Kessler stopped hiring buyers, or if they pushed the program harder. Or if Anna's father's back got worse and he needed me sooner. Family would come first.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time** and no need to scare people.
I'd tell friends it **may never happen**.
think: I'd probably **not act** for a few years, and that's a risk.
At thirty-seven, Anna's father's **plumbing business** would be my obvious next step.
do: Start **weekend work** at the plumbing firm around year three.
Marry next May and **try for children** soon after.
feel: A little **anxious**, because it's **my job** that ends.
S4.quote: I've heard a lot of things promised that never came, but if AGI does come, I don't want to be caught with nothing.
fieldNote: Wei admits he'd **delay acting**, half-doubting it will happen.
His plan rests on **inheriting** a role in his father-in-law's firm.
He'd act sooner if **family needed him** or Kessler stopped hiring.

steps.text: Keep buying at Kessler Drinks and saving each month
Wait until year three before starting weekend plumbing work
Marry next May and try for children soon after

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, with a wedding, no trade, nothing. What would help is apprenticeships for grown men, paid ones, so people like me can learn a trade without losing everything. Not handouts, proper work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. People ask about money and jobs, but a lot of us lean on church and family when things go wrong. That doesn't show up in the numbers.

headlineQuote: People ask about money and jobs, but a lot of us lean on church and family when things go wrong.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old drinks buyer** at a family-owned distributor, engaged to Anna.
He has **never used AI** and checks the ordering program's suggestions by hand.
He accepts a firm's right to cut costs but blames **AI sellers** for overpromising.
He is **anxious or alarmed** whenever thinking AI arrives, expecting to lose buying.
His backup is **family**: an apprenticeship in his future father-in-law's heating firm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, arriving with a wedding and **no trade**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults, as proper work rather than handouts.
